entities.summary:
Arnold of Selenhofen was the archbishop of Mainz from 1153 to his assassination in 1160, playing a pivotal role in the tumultuous politics of the Holy Roman Empire. A member of the powerful Archbishopric of Mainz, Arnold was deeply invested in the theological and political disputes of his time, exemplified by his involvement in the Investiture Controversy. His leadership within the Archbishopric of Mainz had lasting implications for the regional politics of Western Europe. In 1160, Arnold was murdered in the Benedictine abbey St. Jakob, where he had sought refuge from the raging crowd. His death left a power vacuum that would be filled by his successor, Henry the Lion. In the aftermath of Arnold's assassination, the Archbishopric of Mainz was plunged into a period of instability and conflict, with various factions vying for control. The events surrounding Arnold's death and the subsequent power struggles in the Archbishopric of Mainz would have far-reaching consequences for the regional politics of Western Europe.

The events surrounding Arnold's death in 1160 had a profound impact on the regional politics of Western Europe, particularly in the Holy Roman Empire. His murder in the Benedictine abbey St. Jakob marked the beginning of a period of instability and conflict within the Archbishopric of Mainz. The power vacuum created by Arnold's death would be filled by his successor, Henry the Lion, who would go on to play a significant role in shaping the regional politics of Western Europe. In the years following Arnold's assassination, the Holy Roman Empire would experience a period of significant turmoil, with various factions vying for control. The legacy of Arnold of Selenhofen can be seen in the complex web of alliances and rivalries that would shape the regional politics of Western Europe for centuries to come.
